name: WebGL render hash
plain: Renders a fixed 3D scene with custom shaders and hashes the output pixels.
meaning: Floating point and rasterization differences across GPU, driver and ANGLE backend produce a hash that separates devices better than the renderer string, even hardware with the same label.

steps: Draw a gradient or textured triangle

data.metric: Hash of the framebuffer, typically 256x128 px

fields.name: pixel hash
fields.precision: stable per GPU and driver version

limits.headline: Can draw a hidden 3D scene and use the pixels to tell your device apart
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads
can: Draw a fixed 3D scene out of sight
Hash the pixels your graphics card and driver made
Tell devices apart better than the graphics card name alone
Recognise you again on later visits
cannot: Give an exact result when a browser adds noise
Know who you are by itself

story.what_it_is: A script draws a fixed 3D scene with custom shaders and hashes the output pixels.
story.for_you: You see nothing, since the 3D scene is hidden. Your graphics chip and driver draw it with tiny differences, so the result works like a quiet ID for your device.
story.for_makers: This is a strong fingerprint because it depends on hardware, driver and system together. Fraud tools use it to recognize devices. Ad tech uses it to track without cookies.

use_cases.example: A bank draws a hidden 3D scene and compares the hash to the one from your trusted laptop.
A data broker uses the hash to connect your visits across different sites.
A cheater banned from a browser game cannot easily start over, since the device hash matches.
A retailer spots hundreds of new accounts that share the same graphics hash.
A payments company adds the hash to a risk score before approving an order.
A cookie free analytics tool uses the hash to count unique visitors.
A social site finds a bot farm because many fake profiles show the same 3D hash.

technical_bounds: Brave farbling and Safari noise alter readback
